doc.title: Jane Bunnett interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, January 25, 2024

chapter: Women in jazz and being Canadian
title: Women in jazz, Maqueque and Terri Lyne Carrington
summary: She discusses the state of women in jazz, the DownBeat quote on Maqueque, difficult experiences and visa obstacles for her band.

story.theme_name: Race and segregation in the jazz life
story.community_name: Segregation on the road and the bandstand

blocks.x: Does the — are you asked like I’m about to ask you — about the women in jazz, the state of women in jazz?
How do you feel about it right now?
Well I feel great. If there’s a festival it’s a women’s festival that I’m playing at it. If it’s a women’s festival and I’m not playing at it I hate it.

Here’s a quote from a fairly recent DownBeat. I believe it’s about Maqueque. “Band of young killer female musicians play like seasoned veterans. This music is a real treat.” From DownBeat. Do you think we’ll ever get to the point where they could say that same thing but leave out “female”?
And would it be better? Or doesn’t it matter?

Yeah, it probably would be better but you know just at the same — I don’t know. You know I look to somebody like Terri Lyne Carrington to answer those questions and I really admire her because she has been so honest and forthcoming about what she came up through. You know she was a brilliant, talented 10-year-old or however old she was when she, you know her family was like so totally behind her. And you know so many of the musicians took her under their wing which is just marvelous because she’s just like one of the most consummate musicians in the world. And at the same time she totally understands what’s happened and what’s happening for other women that maybe have found it really hard and had to be so hard-nosed and tough to persevere, you know. You know everybody’s story is so different and everybody’s — it’s hard enough, you know, to play jazz and improvised music without having those blocks up, those things in front of you. And it’s still a really hard question for me to answer because I’ve been fortunate in that I surrounded myself with — most of the time — musicians that were extremely kind. I’m talking about male musicians, really kind and generous, and motivated me and inspired me. But it’s not always like that. I mean I’ve had a few experiences but they have been very few where I really have been up against somebody extremely negative and I didn’t feel I conducted myself in the best manner that I could have because I don’t have a skin built up for that and I really lost it and got very angry with the person in a public forum because I was feeling — I won’t go into things but there has been a few things if it’s been a jam session or it’s being in a situation where it felt I was being, you know the hand was coming and I was being — I had no control and that was upsetting. And then there’s also you know sometimes, you know that the thing that happens — now I’m jumping to just the opportunities — if it’s a festival and you hear back now people are very guarded now, they don’t so much talk like this now, but we’ve already got out headline woman performer. You know? So I mean I feel like when we started Maqueque I felt like I was pretty much ahead of the curve of the Me Too movement and in fact I don’t really know really too much about any all-women Latin jazz ensembles, Cuban musicians that are out there. So I felt — I did feel like I was working against that barrier to do some festivals with my group and the tricky thing for me is that entering the U.S., once the band goes into the U.S. with the visa situation I sort of have to stay there. To come back into Canada I have to buy new visas and also have had to petition the State Department to go in with Maqueque to perform in the U.S. Now a couple of my band members are now are American citizens. They applied for asylum there and they got it. But still this is what we’ve been up against, you know up until two years ago just. And that’s really worked against me.
